## Your route {#route}

**Can we attach building information while preserving every original event once?**

An event is not a building. Several events may occur in one building, so
an event identifier and a building matching key do different jobs. We clean the
supplied synthetic event log, state the registry relationship, then inspect
unmatched records before joining.

The final guided audit uses monthly energy: its observation key has two parts.
A valid-looking partial key can multiply rows while every displayed value still
looks plausible.

::: {.callout-note #words}
## Words used in this chapter

| Word or pattern | Meaning here |
|---|---|
| **Observation key** | Identifies one row: `event_id` for an event. |
| **Matching/foreign key** | Links an event to its building; repeated building keys can be legitimate. |
| **Normalization** | Apply an explicit rule treating case/whitespace variants as the same meaning. |
| **Ordered factor** | A categorical variable with a declared progression: low, medium, high. |
| **Parsing** | Interpret text as a typed value, such as a timestamp. |
| **Time zone** | The interpretation of the clock reading; Europe/Paris is the synthetic file convention. |
| **`anti_join`** | Show left-hand rows with no matching right-hand key. |
| **Many-to-one** | Each left-hand row matches at most one right-hand row; zero is allowed. |
| **Composite key** | Several fields together identify the relevant observation, here building plus month. |
:::

## Meeting 1 · Read the computation {#meeting-one}

Class route: two 75-minute meetings, each with its final five-minute exit.

First inspect the raw strings. Normalizing `" bldg-01 "` to `"BLDG-01"`
assumes case and surrounding spaces do not distinguish identifiers. The code
renames raw `building_key` to cleaned `building_id`. That change does not turn
it into the event identifier. A cleaning rule makes a meaning claim and needs
both a syntactic check and later relational evidence.

### Strings, factor levels and timestamps {#stage-1}

**Slide cues:** *Normalize With A Rule*; *Shape Is Not Existence*; *Build And Check The Factor*; *Parse Explicitly*.

The import declares six fields and nine events. `str_squish` removes outer
spaces and compresses repeated inner spaces; case conversion makes the key
format and issue labels consistent. Factor conversion uses the supplied severity
levels rather than alphabetical order. An unexpected label becomes `NA`, so the
check immediately after conversion matters.

`ymd_hm` parses year-month-day and hour-minute with an explicit time zone. It
retains the full timestamp, then derives date, hour and abbreviated month. The
month convention assumes English abbreviations, as in the supplied examples;
if another locale produces different labels, investigate before joining.

**Predict in a private comment first:** BLDG-99 matches the declared identifier pattern. Does that establish a known registry match? What could happen to severity text "urgent" with the declared levels?

<details>
<summary>Compare your reasoning</summary>

No: the pattern checks shape, not membership in the registry. BLDG-99 is
syntactically valid but unknown in this file. "urgent" is not among low, medium,
high, so factor conversion produces NA and the nonmissing-severity check fails.
If your answer differed, distinguish valid syntax from an allowed category or
an actual match.

</details>

**Try before expanding:** Use the Core 3/6 starter to state the cleaning rule, then complete the key and timestamp lines. Compare the original and cleaned fields before opening the reference.

<details>
<summary>Reference version · week10-clean-types_sol.R</summary>

```{r}
#| label: w10-reference-1
# MATH 346 - possible worked solution
# Compare only after attempting the starter; other correct implementations are possible.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(lubridate)

events_path <- "data/week10-service-events.csv"
stopifnot(file.exists(events_path))

events_raw <- read_csv(
  events_path,
  col_types = cols(
    event_id = col_character(),
    building_key = col_character(),
    reported_at = col_character(),
    issue_label = col_character(),
    severity = col_character(),
    response_hours = col_double()
  ),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

expected_raw_names <- c(
  "event_id", "building_key", "reported_at",
  "issue_label", "severity", "response_hours"
)

stopifnot(
  identical(names(events_raw), expected_raw_names),
  nrow(events_raw) == 9,
  n_distinct(events_raw$event_id) == 9,
  nrow(problems(events_raw)) == 0
)

severity_levels <- c("low", "medium", "high")

events <- events_raw |>
  mutate(
    building_id = str_to_upper(str_squish(building_key)),
    issue = str_to_lower(str_squish(issue_label)),
    severity_text = str_to_lower(str_squish(severity)),
    severity = factor(
      severity_text,
      levels = severity_levels,
      ordered = TRUE
    ),
    reported_at = ymd_hm(reported_at, tz = "Europe/Paris", quiet = TRUE),
    report_date = as_date(reported_at),
    report_hour = hour(reported_at),
    month = str_to_lower(format(reported_at, "%b"))
  ) |>
  select(
    event_id, building_id, reported_at, report_date, report_hour,
    month, issue, severity, response_hours
  )

expected_issues <- c("access", "hvac", "lighting", "water leak")

stopifnot(
  all(str_detect(events$building_id, "^BLDG-[0-9]{2}$")),
  identical(sort(unique(events$issue)), sort(expected_issues)),
  is.ordered(events$severity),
  identical(levels(events$severity), severity_levels),
  !any(is.na(events$severity)),
  !any(is.na(events$reported_at)),
  all(events$report_hour >= 0 & events$report_hour <= 23),
  identical(sort(unique(events$month)), c("apr", "feb", "jan", "mar")),
  all(events$response_hours > 0)
)

severity_summary <- events |>
  group_by(severity) |>
  summarize(
    n_events = n(),
    mean_response_hours = mean(response_hours),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

print(events)
print(severity_summary)
cat("Week 10 string, factor, and date-time checks passed.\n")
```

</details>

**Explain / Check / Interpret:** Read the assertions as separate promises: exact issue labels, ordered
severity, no unexpected missing timestamp, valid hours, and four expected months.
The severity summary changes a row from an event to a severity group; group
counts should still account for all nine events. None of these checks alone
confirms registry membership. Preserve the source data for investigating a
conversion failure.

## Meeting 2 · Check the claim {#meeting-two}

A registry row describes one building; an event row describes one report.
The registry lookup should have unique building IDs. Before the join, predict
what duplicated registry keys could do to event multiplicity. The intended
many-to-one relationship prevents multiple matches, but allows unknown keys.
A left join retains the event population; an inner join would change it.

### Audit unmatched rows, then join {#stage-2}

**Slide cues:** *Check Registry Uniqueness*; *Audit Unmatched Events*; *Audit The Other Direction*; *Join With A Contract*; *Post-Join Checks*.

The second reference imports both files and recreates its own event table,
so it does not rely on hidden console objects. Read the two `anti_join` calls in
opposite directions. Unknown event buildings and registered buildings without
an event are different populations.

The left join matches on cleaned `building_id` and declares many-to-one. It
keeps the unmatched event with missing registry fields. The later `coalesce`
labels that missing zone "unmatched" for the summary; it does not invent a
registry match. Keep the unmatched record visible while investigating.

**Predict · Think first:** The registry has six buildings and the log has nine events. Should the joined result have six rows? How many records should the two unmatched tables contain?

<details>
<summary>Compare your reasoning</summary>

The left-hand event population has nine rows. There is one unknown event,
EVT-008 at BLDG-99, and one registered building with no event, BLDG-06. Those two
one-row unmatched tables answer different questions. If your answer differed,
you may have counted buildings rather than events, or reversed the join direction.

</details>

**Try before expanding:** Complete Core 7/8/9 in the starter: check lookup multiplicity and inspect unmatched rows before running the join.

<details>
<summary>Reference version · week10-join-audit_sol.R</summary>

```{r}
#| label: w10-reference-2
# MATH 346 - possible worked solution
# Compare only after attempting the starter; other correct implementations are possible.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(lubridate)

registry_path <- "data/week10-building-registry.csv"
events_path <- "data/week10-service-events.csv"
stopifnot(file.exists(registry_path), file.exists(events_path))

registry <- read_csv(
  registry_path,
  col_types = cols(
    building_id = col_character(),
    building_name = col_character(),
    campus_zone = col_character(),
    building_type = col_character()
  ),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

events_raw <- read_csv(
  events_path,
  col_types = cols(
    event_id = col_character(),
    building_key = col_character(),
    reported_at = col_character(),
    issue_label = col_character(),
    severity = col_character(),
    response_hours = col_double()
  ),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

events <- events_raw |>
  transmute(
    event_id,
    building_id = str_to_upper(str_squish(building_key)),
    reported_at = ymd_hm(reported_at, tz = "Europe/Paris", quiet = TRUE),
    issue = str_to_lower(str_squish(issue_label)),
    severity = factor(
      str_to_lower(str_squish(severity)),
      levels = c("low", "medium", "high"),
      ordered = TRUE
    ),
    response_hours
  )

registry_key_counts <- registry |>
  count(building_id, name = "registry_rows")

stopifnot(
  nrow(registry) == 6,
  nrow(registry_key_counts) == nrow(registry),
  all(registry_key_counts$registry_rows == 1),
  n_distinct(events$event_id) == nrow(events)
)

unmatched_events <- events |>
  anti_join(registry, by = "building_id")

buildings_without_events <- registry |>
  anti_join(events, by = "building_id")

event_buildings <- events |>
  left_join(
    registry,
    by = "building_id",
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  )

stopifnot(
  nrow(event_buildings) == nrow(events),
  n_distinct(event_buildings$event_id) == nrow(events),
  identical(unmatched_events$event_id, "EVT-008"),
  identical(buildings_without_events$building_id, "BLDG-06"),
  sum(is.na(event_buildings$building_name)) == 1,
  sum(!is.na(event_buildings$building_name)) == 8
)

zone_summary <- event_buildings |>
  mutate(campus_zone = coalesce(campus_zone, "unmatched")) |>
  count(campus_zone, name = "n_events") |>
  arrange(campus_zone)

stopifnot(sum(zone_summary$n_events) == nrow(events))

print(unmatched_events)
print(buildings_without_events)
print(zone_summary)
cat("Week 10 join contract passed without row multiplication.\n")
```

</details>

**Explain / Check / Interpret:** The source checks nine unique event IDs, eight nonmissing building names
and one missing building name. The zone-summary counts sum to nine. Also compare
the original ID set and event response values when evaluating preservation:
count and uniqueness alone cannot exclude substitution of one ID for another.
A many-to-one declaration protects multiplicity, not whether the chosen key
has the intended meaning.

## AI audit · Inspect before accepting {#ai-audit}

**Slide cues:** *A Plausible AI Join*; *The Missing Key Component*; *Repair The Join*.

This is **selective Guided practice**; use it when selected or helpful.

Read the supplied target and choose a check before opening the diagnosis.
No AI service is contacted.

The source includes both a flawed join and its repair. First inspect only
the building-only join; stop reading at `generated_event_counts` until you have
predicted multiplicity. Candidate checks: nine rows, nine distinct event IDs,
one row per event, complete building-month matching key. The generated
`many-to-many` declaration accepts row multiplication rather than fixing it.

**Reading excerpt:** this fragment relies on the supplied script setup; inspect it here, then run the complete file in the evidence reveal.

```r
generated_join <- events |>
  left_join(
    energy_long,
    by = "building_id",
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  )
```


**Predict in a private comment first:** Eight known events each find four monthly rows and one unknown event has no match. How many left-join rows result, and which key component is missing?

<details>
<summary>Compare your reasoning</summary>

There are `8 * 4 + 1 = 33` rows. The energy row is one building-month,
so month must join building_id in the matching key. The repaired join returns
nine event rows. If your answer differed, remember that a left join still emits
one unmatched row; it does not emit zero rows for that event. Inspect both
multiplicity and missing attached information before interpreting energy.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Run the complete supplied critique target and inspect the evidence</summary>

```{r}
#| label: w10-reference-ai
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(lubridate)

events_path <- "data/week10-service-events.csv"
energy_path <- "data/week09-campus-energy-wide.csv"
stopifnot(file.exists(events_path), file.exists(energy_path))

events_raw <- read_csv(
  events_path,
  col_types = cols(
    event_id = col_character(),
    building_key = col_character(),
    reported_at = col_character(),
    issue_label = col_character(),
    severity = col_character(),
    response_hours = col_double()
  ),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

energy_wide <- read_csv(
  energy_path,
  na = c("", "missing"),
  col_types = cols(
    building_id = col_character(),
    building_type = col_character(),
    area_m2 = col_double(),
    jan_kwh = col_double(),
    feb_kwh = col_double(),
    mar_kwh = col_double(),
    apr_kwh = col_double()
  ),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

events <- events_raw |>
  transmute(
    event_id,
    building_id = str_to_upper(str_squish(building_key)),
    reported_at = ymd_hm(reported_at, tz = "Europe/Paris", quiet = TRUE),
    month = str_to_lower(format(reported_at, "%b")),
    response_hours
  )

energy_long <- energy_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = ends_with("_kwh"),
    names_to = "month",
    names_pattern = "(.*)_kwh",
    values_to = "energy_kwh"
  )

# Generated code accepts a many-to-many join and uses only building_id.
# Every matched event is therefore repeated once for each energy month.
generated_join <- events |>
  left_join(
    energy_long,
    by = "building_id",
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  )

generated_event_counts <- generated_join |>
  count(event_id, name = "rows_after_join")

stopifnot(
  nrow(events) == 9,
  nrow(generated_join) == 33,
  all(generated_event_counts$rows_after_join[generated_event_counts$event_id != "EVT-008"] == 4),
  generated_event_counts$rows_after_join[generated_event_counts$event_id == "EVT-008"] == 1
)

# The repaired join uses the full building-month observation key.
repaired_join <- events |>
  left_join(
    energy_long,
    by = c("building_id", "month"),
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  )

stopifnot(
  nrow(repaired_join) == nrow(events),
  n_distinct(repaired_join$event_id) == nrow(events),
  sum(is.na(repaired_join$building_type)) == 1,
  sum(is.na(repaired_join$energy_kwh)) == 1
)

print(generated_event_counts)
cat("The generated join expands 9 events to 33 rows.\n")
cat("The repaired building-month join preserves 9 event observations.\n")
```

</details>

### Meeting 2 in-class exit · Final five minutes

What evidence shows that a join preserved the intended observation unit?

Solo readers: use the self-check below; no submission.

### Meeting 2 self-check · No submission

Close earlier reveals and explain from memory: A declared many-to-one left join preserves nine events but one has no
building match. Did the declaration fail? Would an inner join preserve the same
population?

<details>
<summary>Compare the Meeting 2 self-check</summary>

The declaration can pass: many-to-one means at most one match, including
zero. The left join keeps the unknown event. An inner join would remove it and
leave eight events in this supplied case. Match coverage and multiplicity need
separate checks; the unknown event is not automatically erroneous.

</details>
